107.t: Detroit's black community and its musical vibrancy
107.s: Foster describes the huge black neighborhoods, so unlike Cincinnati, and links them to the energy of the scene.
107.q: I definitely think that that’s connected to the vibrancy, as you say. There was a large black community. I used to ride for blocks on a bus or a streetcar down one street, and for ten to 15 minutes I’d be riding through a black community. I would be amazed, because in Cincinnati, if you’re riding…

107.s: Foster says the lively Detroit scene explains how Motown arose, unlike Cincinnati.
107.q: I couldn’t see it at the time, but I can perfectly understand now retroactively to 1965, how Motown would come out of that.

506.s: Detroit had several major clubs; Carter's first road gig was with Chico Hamilton at the Club Saturn, with Ahmad Jamal and T-Bone Walker nearby.
506.q: Oh yeah. There were three or four major clubs that brought in major acts. And when I left Detroit and went away to school, the first gig I had on the road was at a club at Detroit that’s called the Club Saturn, with Chico Hamilton’s band; and cross town was Ahmad Jamal’s band and about eight blocks…

581.t: Detroit as a nurturing environment for musicians
581.s: Detroit's many great musicians and the idea that you create an environment in which people learn.
581.ch: Detroit and the Bop and Locke act
581.q: Oh boy, it was quite an environment. It was wonderful. It was sharing. You know, they said, I heard a guy say one time, I don’t know what his name is, I always mix him up with, he played, in Malcolm X he played Elijah Muhammad. I could never — he teaches out at Howard University. I can’t think of…

838.t: Growing up in Detroit and its club scene
838.s: Born in Kansas City, raised in Detroit from age two; many black and tan clubs in the late 30s and early 40s.
838.q: Yes. One of the most. It was a tremendous amount of jazz music in Detroit at that time. There were so many clubs, oh, that was before we hit the “great white jackpot.”

503.t: What was in the water in Detroit: migration, jobs and instruments
503.s: Burrell says Detroit's jazz talent grew from migration for auto work, family income to buy instruments, and opportunity.
503.q: I don’t think I have any special insight. I think what I might say has probably already been said and said by people that are none musicians. That there was a migration from the south to places like Chicago and Detroit and Detroit in particular because of the automobile industry. And so a lot of…

144.t: Detroit's musical families and show-town clubs
144.s: Asked about the McKinney family, Fuller names the Grey family and describes the Detroit population and show lounges.
144.q: There were other families, the Grey family. Ken Grey, he was playing “Firedance” and all that stuff. Classical—Detroit had an abundance of young blacks. There were no Spanish there, and not in the town I grew up in. It was either white or black when I came up. Now, it’s a little bit of everything.…

371.t: Why so many Detroit musicians recorded in the late 1940s and 1950s
371.s: Jones has no explanation for the outpouring of Detroit talent and thinks the 'Detroit sound' was a writer's phrase.
371.ch: 1950s clubs, Savoy dates and the Detroit sound
371.q: I don't know how to get started but the description that you gave earlier on, some writer did that I guess, I don't know. Maybe it, in away, impressed him. Maybe he was just trying to think up some clever thing to say. You know, there are pianists who come from other cities who also play that…

576.t: Finding the Club Sudan and meeting Skeeter Spight and Leroy Mitchell
576.s: In Detroit she finds the Club Sudan, meets Tommy, Barry, Kenny and the scat singers Skeeter Spight and Leroy Mitchell, and her friend Jackie Berkhoff.
576.q: We… you know what? At the time, I think they were segregated. But, but I found a way, you know, I found a way to find out where these guys were playing, where this music was happening „cause I knew it had to be happening. So uh, and I did. I found the Club Sudan, which was a place that a white…

235.t: Living near the Carlton Hotel; Matthew Gee and Johnny Austin
235.s: He lived across from the club, met Matthew Gee and Johnny Austin, and recalls Illinois Jacquet's Flying Home and talk of Dizzy around 1941.
235.q: across the street. And...I think it was the Carlton Hotel and there was plenty of places to eat right in there and the musicians were there all the time and the different bands were comin' in. I think the Alabama State Collegians with the Trenier twins were workin' up the street and that's when I…
